Fixing Apollo for Lamda Components

Why the current filters return breweries and food-delivery firms, what to search instead, and how to run the whole campaign inside Apollo without touching a CSV.

Prepared 31 July 2026 Tested live in Apollo For Lamda Components Pvt. Ltd.

The short version

The current filter set describes a job title in a large Indian company. It never describes what the company manufactures. That single gap is why the list is full of businesses that will never buy an aluminium casting.

Adding one filter cuts the list by 89% and replaces caterers and logistics firms with pump, motor and appliance makers. Everything else in this document follows from that.

Why this happens

Every large company employs procurement managers. A waffle chain buys flour, a brewery buys bottles, a property developer buys cement. Filtering on the job title alone finds all of them equally well. The filter has no way of knowing Lamda sells castings.

02

Adding what the company makes

One filter — Company Keywords — does most of the work.

Same titles, same location, same size. The only change is three keywords describing the customer's industry rather than the contact's job.

Before
21,672
Titles only
After
5,515
Titles + 3 keywords
Removed
75%
Almost entirely waste
But look closely — this is still not right

Bristlecone, TVS Supply Chain Solutions and Xpressbees are consulting and logistics companies. They appear because the phrase “supply chain” sits in the job titles being searched. They buy software and warehousing, not castings.

03

The search built around what Lamda sells

Sector keywords taken from Lamda's own product page.

Lamda's website lists the sectors its castings go into. Automotive is only one of them:

Fuel injection pumpsAlternators & starter motors EV motorsTextile machinery Hydraulic equipmentPneumatic products LED lights & door closuresHousehold appliances Medical equipmentWhite goods Off-road products

The company-size filter was also lowered. Lamda runs 250–800 tonne machines with a small team; a 2,000+ employee floor screens out exactly the mid-size manufacturers most likely to place an order this year.

Important — remove your own competitors

This list still contains Esko Casting, Aakar Foundry, Sound Castings, Roots Cast and Endurance Technologies. Those are foundries and die casters. The keyword die casting finds companies that perform die casting, not companies that buy it.

Fix: drop that keyword, or add the casting firms under Company → Exclude so they never reappear.

04

The named OEMs are a separate exercise

Toyota, Tata Motors, Bosch and the rest need their own list.

None of the searches above target those ten companies — no company-name filter was applied. Reaching a fixed list of named accounts is a different motion: you don't want volume, you want the right twenty or thirty people inside ten businesses.

Named-account search — the ten OEMs 
https://app.apollo.io/#/people?page=1&contactEmailStatusV2[]=verified&personTitles[]=purchase%20manager&personTitles[]=procurement%20manager&personTitles[]=sourcing%20manager&personTitles[]=supply%20chain%20manager&personTitles[]=head%20of%20procurement&personTitles[]=vendor%20development&qOrganizationName[]=Toyota&qOrganizationName[]=Tata%20Motors&qOrganizationName[]=Kia&qOrganizationName[]=Honda&qOrganizationName[]=Royal%20Enfield&qOrganizationName[]=Uno%20Minda&qOrganizationName[]=Bosch&qOrganizationName[]=Ashok%20Leyland&qOrganizationName[]=Ather&qOrganizationName[]=Delta%20Electronics

Vendor Development has been added to the job titles. At Indian OEMs that is usually the function that onboards and qualifies a new casting supplier — often a better first contact than procurement.

One observation worth checking internally

Lamda's published case study describes supplying lifting brackets to Toyota Industries India — 15,000 components a month, fitted to textile machinery. Toyota Industries is a separate business from Toyota Motor. If the reference account is a machinery manufacturer, the prospect list should look like machinery manufacturers.

05

Saving a list — no download required

Answering “can we use the contacts without the CSV?”

Yes. Selecting contacts in the search results reveals an action bar with everything needed. The export button is there, but nothing requires it.

  1. Run the searchUse the URL in section 3, or rebuild the filters by hand.
  2. Select the contactsTick individual rows, or the header checkbox to take the whole page.
  3. Add to listChoose Add to list and either pick an existing list or create one — for example “Pumps & Motors — Q3”.
  4. Save the search itselfSave search at the top keeps the filters. Apollo then shows a Net New count each time you return — contacts that have appeared since you last looked.
Why this matters beyond convenience

Once contacts live in Apollo rather than a spreadsheet, replies, opens, bounces and unsubscribes attach to the record. A CSV cannot tell you who replied, and cannot stop the same person being emailed twice from two different exports.

06

Using a saved list to launch a sequence

The step that replaces the download and re-upload entirely.

Lists you have already built stay available everywhere in Apollo. Selecting contacts and choosing Add to list shows them all, with live counts, split across All lists · My lists · Team lists.

The same selection can go straight into outreach. Sequence in the action bar offers four destinations:

Working the other way — starting from a list rather than a search — the Lists filter at the top of the left rail loads any saved list back into the results view, where the same action bar applies:

  1. Open the listLeft rail → Lists → Select lists… → choose the list.
  2. Select the contactsHeader checkbox takes the whole page; Apollo then offers to select every contact in the list.
  3. Send them to a sequenceSequence → Add to existing Sequence, or Add to new Sequence to build one now.
  4. Confirm the sending mailboxApollo asks which mailbox sends and at what schedule, then starts the contacts on step 1.
What this replaces

Today: download CSV → open the outreach platform → map columns → import → hope nothing was emailed last month. In Apollo it is one menu, and anyone already in another sequence, already replied, or already unsubscribed is excluded automatically.

07

Running the campaign from inside Apollo

Sequences: the part that replaces the separate outreach tool.

A sequence is an automated series of touches — emails, calls, LinkedIn actions — with delays between each. Contacts flow into it straight from a list or from search results.

A workable structure for a casting enquiry

Day 0 — automatic email, the introduction. Day 3 — LinkedIn view profile (manual, no message). Day 5 — automatic follow-up referencing a specific component. Day 9 — phone call task. Day 14 — final short email.

Anyone who replies drops out automatically. That is the behaviour a CSV and a generic mail tool cannot reproduce.

08

Follow-ups that change by role and company

The third question — sending the right message to the right person.

The controls in that screenshot answer the question directly:

ControlWhat it doesUse it for
Email typeOutreach, Follow-up or Last pitch Later steps automatically read as follow-ups rather than repeat introductions
Recent company newsPulls current news about the prospect's employer New plant, new model launch, capacity expansion — reasons to need a casting supplier
Relevant job postingsReads their open roles A company hiring production engineers is scaling manufacturing
Executive Persona ResearchAdapts to the individual's seniority A Purchase Manager and a Head of Procurement get different framing
Strategic Company ResearchPulls the company's stated priorities Localisation, cost reduction, import substitution
ToneDefault, Direct, Formal, Casual, Creative, Custom Formal for OEM procurement; direct for smaller manufacturers

In the screenshot, Apollo has drafted a mail for a named contact at Shriram Pistons that references that company's specific situation. That is per-contact personalisation applied across a list of thousands — the thing a mail-merge from a CSV cannot do.

Simplest way to segment

Build one list per sector — Pumps & Motors, Textile Machinery, Medical Devices, Appliances — and run a separate sequence for each, with the opening line naming a component Lamda already makes for that sector. Same effort, materially better reply rates than one generic campaign.

09

One thing to set up before sending

Sequences are built and ready; they need an outbox.

  • Link the sending mailbox. Settings → Mailboxes & domains, then connect the Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 account the team already sends from.
  • Use a real person's mailbox — a named individual, not info@ or sales@. Replies to a person get answered; replies to a shared inbox get ignored.
  • Consider a separate sending domain for cold outreach, so any deliverability damage never touches the main company domain.
Before the first send

Warm the mailbox for two to three weeks at low volume, keep to roughly 30–50 mails a day per inbox to begin with, and make sure SPF, DKIM and DMARC are set on the sending domain. A brand-new mailbox sending hundreds of cold mails on day one lands in spam and damages the domain for months.
